practice.security_practice: Separate all environments used in software development
practice.outcome:
All environments used in software development, including development, build, 
test, and distribution environments, are separated from each other to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data and systems.
practice.risk_addressed: Reduce the risk of lateral movement or privilege escalation between development and sensitive business environments.
practice.recommend_action: All software development environments should be logically separated from each other and enforced via controls such as network segmentation and access controls.

practice.security_practice: Regularly log, monitor, and review trust relationships used for authorization and access across software development environments
practice.outcome: All software development environments and tooling have associated logging and monitoring mechanisms.
practice.risk_addressed: Lateral movement, privilege escalation, insider threats, data exfiltration.
practice.recommend_action: Perform a review of all software development environments and tooling to verify associated logging capabilities and functions are enabled.

practice.security_practice: Enforce MFA across software development environments
practice.outcome: Users are required to authenticate into software development environments with MFA.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, code misconfigurations, outdated code dependencies
practice.recommend_action: Require MFA (ideally phishing-resistant MFA) to access all software development environments.

practice.security_practice: Establish and enforce security requirements for software products used across software development environments
practice.outcome: Organizations have defined processes, policies, and procedures for managing risks of software products used across software development environments.
practice.risk_addressed: Misconfigurations, Shadow IT, supply chain vulnerabilities, insecure code
practice.recommend_action: Document processes, policies, and procedures for managing risks of software products used across software development environments. Maintain, replace, and remove software in accordance with policies, processes, and procedures.Assess the authenticity and integrity of software prior to use in environments.

practice.security_practice: Securely store and transmit credentials used in software development environments
practice.outcome: Organizations have eliminated the insecure storage and transmission of plaintext credentials.
practice.risk_addressed: Lateral movement, privilege escalation, insider threats, data exfiltration
practice.recommend_action: Do not store sensitive data or credentials in source code. Instead, store sensitive data and credentials in an encrypted manner, such as using a secret manager.Securely store and rotate SSH keys.

practice.security_practice: Implement effective perimeter and internal network monitoring solutions with streamlined, real-time alerting to aid responses to suspected and confirmed cyber incidents
practice.outcome: The organization monitors environments to determine the presence of indicators of compromise (IOCs).  Upon determination of suspected or actual IOCs, the incident response playbook is activated.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, lateral movement, command and control (C2), privilege escalation, data exfiltration, insider threats
practice.recommend_action: Establish an incident response playbook with criteria for declaring incidents, along with protocols that clearly define roles, responsibilities, and identifies stakeholders who require notification.Designate an enterprise incident response team and conduct frequent table top exercises.

practice.security_practice: Establish a software supply chain risk management program
practice.outcome: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management practices are integrated into the SDLC.
practice.risk_addressed: Code tampering, outdated code dependencies, data breaches
practice.recommend_action: Conduct code testing and audit software supply chain practices and document the activities conducted.

practice.security_practice: Make a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) available to customers
practice.outcome: Customers should be provided with documentation that demonstrates component provenance.
practice.risk_addressed: Code tampering, outdated code dependencies, data breaches
practice.recommend_action: Develop a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and provide it to customers with each product.

practice.security_practice: Inspect source code for vulnerabilities through automated tools or comparable processes and mitigate known vulnerabilities prior to any release of products, versions, or update releases
practice.outcome: Security testing is conducted in a codified, repeatable, and time sensitive fashion on new and current products.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, code misconfigurations, outdated code dependencies
practice.recommend_action: Perform Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), and Software Composition Analysis (SCA) where appropriate.

practice.security_practice: Address identified vulernabilities prior to product release
practice.outcome: Identification of vulnerabilities prior to release triggers an action to either remediate or address the vulnerability before release.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, code misconfigurations, outdated code dependencies
practice.recommend_action: Develop, maintain, and execute a process or policy that governs actions to take upon identification of a security vulnerability prior to a product release.

practice.outcome: Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy that meets the defined criteria.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, code misconfigurations, outdated code dependencies
practice.recommend_action: Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy (VDP) that authorizes testing by members of the public on products offered by the manufacturer, commits to not recommending or pursuing legal action against anyone engaging in good faith efforts to follow the VDP, provides a clear channel to report vulnerabilities, and allows for public disclosure of vulnerabilities in line with coordinated vulnerability disclosure best practices and international standards.Address disclosed software vulnerabilities in a timely fashion.

practice.security_practice: Increase the use of multifactor authentication (MFA)
practice.outcome: More users use MFA to authenticate.
practice.risk_addressed: Reduce the risk of password compromise or utilization of weak passwords.
practice.recommend_action: Increase the use of MFA, such as by implementing enabling MFA (ideally, phishing-resistant MFA) by default for users and administrators.Implementing “seat belt chimes” in products to nudge users towards enabling MFA. This could include, banners or interstitials notifying users or administrators that MFA is not enabled or suggesting that administrators enable phishing-resistant MFA.Supporting standards-based single sign-on (SSO) in the baseline version of the product, allowing customers to configure with their own identity provider that supports MFA.

practice.outcome: The product does not use default passwords.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries may leverage manufacturer or supplier set default credentials on control system devices.
practice.recommend_action:
Eliminate default passwords from the organization's software products. Instead, take an alternate approach, such as:

Providing random, instance-unique initial passwords for the product.Requiring the user who installs the product to create a strong password at the start of the installation process.Providing time-limited setup passwords that disable themselves when a setup process is complete and require configuration of a secure password (or more secure authentication approaches, such as phishing-resistant MFA).Requiring physical access for initial setup and the specification of instance-unique credentials.Conducting campaigns or offering updates that transition existing deployments from default passwords to more secure authentication mechanisms.

practice.outcome: Organizations should  proactively reduce systemic classes of vulnerabilities.
practice.risk_addressed: Code tampering, outdated code dependencies, data breaches
practice.recommend_action:
Take approaches to work towards reduce entire classes of vulnerabilities, such as:

Implement parameterized queries to reduce SQL injection vulnerabilities.Transition to utilizing memory safe languages to reduce memory safety vulnerabilities.Utilize web template frameworks to reduce cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.

practice.security_practice: Provide customers with security patching in a timely manner
practice.outcome: Security patches are offered on a widespread basis to customers.
practice.risk_addressed:
Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral 
movement
practice.recommend_action: Provide security patches to customers in a timely manner and on a widespread basis.

practice.security_practice: Ensure customers understand when products are nearing end of life support and security patches will no longer be provided
practice.outcome: Users understand when software is no longer supported and will transition to supported products.
practice.risk_addressed:
Inadequate patching of software vulnerabilities exposes systems to significant 
risk
practice.recommend_action:
Notify customers and confirm receipt of notification stating 
product(s) are nearing end of life support and security patches will no longer be provided.

practice.security_practice: Include Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) and Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) fields in every Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) record for the organization's products.
practice.outcome: CVEs that meet the defined criteria are published and CWE and CPE fields are included in all CVEs
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, code misconfigurations, outdated code dependencies
practice.recommend_action:
Include accurate Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) and Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) fields in every Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) record for the organization's products. Additionally, 
issue CVEs in a timely manner for, at minimum, all critical or high impact vulnerabilities (whether discovered internally or by a third party) that either require actions by a customer to patch or have evidence of active exploitation.

practice.security_practice: Increase the ability for customers to gather evidence of cybersecurity intrusions affecting the organization's products
practice.outcome: Customers have access and ability to monitor and respond to intrusions affecting the product
practice.risk_addressed: Initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement
practice.recommend_action: Verify whether all products, to the extent possible, have logging capabilities

practice.security_practice: Monitor Supply Chain Incident Reporting & Vulnerability Disclosures
practice.outcome: Organizations more rapidly learn about and respond to known incidents or breaches across vendors and service providers.
practice.scope: Third party vendors and service providers
practice.risk_addressed: Insufficient Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management (C-SCRM) practices that cannot securely support the organization's technologies & processes.
practice.recommend_action:
Procurement documents and contracts, such as service-level agreements (SLAs), stipulate that vendors and/or service providers notify the procuring customer of security incidents within a risk-informed time frame as determined by the organization.Organization with OT assets need to document and track serial numbers, checksums, digital certificates/signatures or other 
identifying features that can enable them to verify the authenticity of vendor-provided OT hardware, software and firmware.

practice.outcome:
The organization’s cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations, and policies are established, communicated, and monitored to identify 
any necessary adjustments.
practice.risk_addressed: Insufficient cybersecurity policies and procedures/practices that can securely support the organization's technologies & processes.
practice.recommend_action: Policies for managing the cybersecurity program are reviewed, updated, communicated, and enforced to reflect changes in requirements, threats, technology, and organizational mission. Policies are established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities are communicated and enforced.  It is recommended that organizational governance encompass the policies, procedures, and processes necessary to manage the organization’s regulatory, legal, risk, environmental, and operational obligations.OT-specific policies and proceedures should consider the limitations of existing IT cybersecurity program to identify priorities for critical operational functions, OT-specific security concerns and compensating controls.

practice.security_practice: Govern Risks from Managed Service Providers (MSPs)
practice.outcome: The risks posed by an MSP are identified, recorded, assessed, prioritized, monitored, and updated over the course of the relationship.
practice.scope: Service providers that remotely manage an organization's IT and/or OT infrastructure, cyber security, and/or other related business operations.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries can exploit organizations with access to their targets by abusing trusted third-party relationships.
practice.recommend_action: Develop and maintain a thorough understanding of the services including security products a MSP and/or external vendors/integrators are providing via the contractual arrangement and address any security requirements that fall outside the scope of the contract.

practice.outcome: A maintained asset inventory to improve cybersecurity resilience by reducing downtime, aiding recovery, bolstering defenses, and improving preparedness.
practice.scope:
Data, Hardware, Software,
Systems, Facilities, Personnel
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries might use computer accessories, networking hardware, or other devices as entry points to infiltrate systems or networks.
practice.recommend_action: Maintain a regularly updated inventory of all organizational assets (i.e.  data, hardware, software, systems, facilities, and personnel).   IT and OT assets determined to be critical for business or operational functions are updated on a more frequent  basis.

practice.outcome: Reduced likelihood of threat actors exploiting known vulnerabilities to breach organizational networks.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries might exploit vulnerabilities in an Internet-facing host or system, such as software bugs, temporary glitches, or misconfigurations, to gain initial access to a network.
practice.recommend_action: Implement vulnerability management technologies to patch and mitigate misconfigured software in a timely manner. Monitor risk response progress through tools like  plan of action and milestones (POA&M), risk registers, and risk detail reports. Document potential risks of proposed changes and provide rollback guidance. Assign responsibilities and ensure procedures are followed for processing and responding to cybersecurity threats, vulnerabilities, or incident disclosures from various stakeholders. Incorporate compensating security controls (i.e., defense in depth) to address legacy systems where possible.

practice.security_practice: Obtain Independent Validation of Cybersecurity Controls
practice.outcome: Ability to identify TTPs that lack proper defenses, and establish confidence in organizational cyber defenses.
practice.scope: Internal and external organizational assets and networks
practice.risk_addressed: Reduce risk of gaps in cyber defenses or a false sense of security in existing protections.
practice.recommend_action: Organizations regularly engage third-party cybersecurity experts to validate their defenses through various exercises, to include penetration tests, bug bounties, incident simulations, and table-top exercises. These tests, both announced and unannounced, assess the ability of external and internal adversaries to infiltrate and move laterally within the network, targeting critical systems. High-impact findings from these tests are promptly addressed to prevent recurrence.

practice.outcome: Identify improvements by practicing cybersecurity & Incident response plans to maintain and update the organization’s cybersecurity program.
practice.risk_addressed:
Inability to 
quickly and effectively  isolate, contain, eradicate, remediate, and communicate about cybersecurity incidents.
practice.recommend_action:
Organizations have, maintain, update, and regularly drill IT and OT cybersecurity incident response plans for both common and organizationally-specific (e.g., by sector, locality) threat scenarios and TTPs. When conducted, tests or drills are as realistic as feasible. Drill IR plans at least annually, and update within a risk-informed time frame following the lessons learned portion 
of any exercise, drill, or real world event.OT IR plans, account for specific safety and containment considerations which differ from existing IT plans and priorities.

practice.outcome: Prevent threat actors from using default passwords to achieve initial access or move laterally in a network.
practice.scope: Password-protected newly acquired and legacy IT and OT assets.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries might acquire and exploit default account credentials to gain initial access, maintain persistence, escalate privileges, or evade defenses.
practice.recommend_action:
Implement a organization-wide policy that requires changing default manufacturer passwords for all hardware, software, and firmware before connecting them to any internal or external network. This includes IT assets used in OT, such as OT administration web pages.If changing default passwords is not feasible (e.g., due to hard-coded passwords in control systems), document and implement appropriate compensating security controls and monitor logs for network traffic and login attempts on these devices.For OT: Changing default passwords on existing OT systems is 
more labor-intensive, recommend establishing a policy for changing default credentials on all new or future devices. This will reduce potential risk in the future if vulnerabilities change.

practice.outcome: Protect organizations from automated, credential-based attacks.
practice.scope: Password-protected assets, where safe and technically capable
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers may attempt to access accounts by guessing passwords without prior knowledge of legitimate credentials. They might use repetitive methods and lists of common passwords, sometimes disregarding password complexity policies. However, this approach risks numerous authentication failures and potential account lockouts based on the organization's policies.
practice.recommend_action: All unsuccessful logins are logged and sent to an organization's security team or relevant logging system. Security teams are notified (e.g., by an alert) after a specific number of consecutive unsuccessful login attempts in a short period and a deviation from normal user behavior. This alert is logged and stored in the relevant security or ticketing system for retroactive analysis. For IT assets, a system-enforced policy prevents future logins for the suspicious account. For example, this could be for some minimum time, or until the account is re-enabled by a privileged user. This configuration is enabled when available on an asset.

practice.outcome: Add a critical, additional layer of security to protect assets accounts whose credentials have been compromised.
practice.scope: Organizational ssets with remote access, such as workstations and human-machine interfaces (HMIs), where safe and technically capable
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers without prior knowledge of legitimate credentials might try commonly used passwords across various accounts to gain access. They might also systematically guess passwords using repetitive or iterative methods.
practice.recommend_action:
Organizations require MFA for access to assets using the strongest available 
method, if MFA is available for that asset. MFA options sorted by strength, high to low, are as follows:1. Phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO/WebAuthn or public key infrastructure (PKI)-based – see CISA guidance in “Resources”).2. If Phishing-resistant MFA is not available, then mobile app-based soft tokens (preferably push notification with number matching).3. MFA via short message service (SMS) or voice only used when no other options are possible.IT: All IT accounts leverage MFA to access organizational resources. Prioritize accounts with highest risk, such as privileged administrative accounts for key IT systems.OT:  MFA is enabled on all accounts and systems that can be accessed remotely, including vendors/maintenance accounts, remotely accessible user and engineering workstations, and remotely accessible HMIs when available.   If MFA is not available, remove remote access, introduce additional segmentation steps and credential management should be prioritized.

practice.outcome: Make it harder for threat actors to gain access to administrator or privileged accounts, even if common user accounts are compromised.
practice.scope: Organizational assets, where safe and technically capable
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers might obtain and exploit credentials from existing accounts for initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion. These compromised credentials can bypass network access controls and provide continuous access to remote systems and external services.
practice.recommend_action: User accounts do not have administrator privileges. Administrators maintain separate user accounts for activities unrelated to their admin role, such as business email and web browsing. Privileges are revaluated on a recurring basis to validate continued need for a given set of permissions.

practice.outcome: Reduce the likelihood of adversaries accessing segmented networks if the primary enterprise network is compromised.
practice.scope: Organizational assets, where safe and technically capable
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers are able to gather details about device communication patterns and may also attempt to list services on remote hosts and local network devices, identifying ones vulnerable to remote software exploitation.
practice.recommend_action: All connections to OT and/or other segmented networks are denied by default unless explicitly allowed (e.g., by IP address and port) for specific system functionality. Necessary communications paths between the primary enterprise network and isolated networks must pass through an intermediary, such as a properly configured firewall, bastion host, "jump box," or a demilitarized zone, which is closely monitored, captures network logs, and only allows connections from approved assets. When applicable physically segment OT networks.

practice.outcome: Organizational users learn and perform more secure behaviors.
practice.scope: All employees, contractors, partners, suppliers, providers,  and all other users of the organization's non-public resources.
practice.risk_addressed: Train users on recognizing access or manipulation attempts by attackers to lower the risk of successful spearphishing, social engineering, and other techniques that involve user interaction.
practice.recommend_action: At least annual trainings for all organizational users to train personnel to recognize social engineering attempts and other common attacks, how to properly report attacks and suspicious activity, comply with acceptable use policies, and perform basic cyber hygiene tasks (e.g., choosing passwords, protecting credentials).Identify the specialized roles within the organization that require additional cybersecurity training, such as physical and cybersecurity personnel, system administrators, finance personnel, senior leadership, and anyone with access to business-critical data. Provide role-based cybersecurity training to all those in specialized roles, including contractors, partners, suppliers, and other third parties.Personnel should receive security awareness and training for the OT environment and specific application. In addition, organizations should identify, document and train all personnel who have significant OT roles and responsibilities.New employees receive initial cybersecurity training within 10 days of onboarding and recurring training on at least an annual basis.

practice.outcome: Effective encryption deployed to maintain confidentiality of sensitive data and integrity on the organization's network.
practice.scope: All IT traffic and remote OT assets (those that communicate with external entities)
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers can position themselves between networked devices to enable network sniffing, data manipulation, or other attacks.
practice.recommend_action: Use encryption, digital signatures, and cryptographic hashes to protect the confidentiality and integrity of network communications.  OT:  Use encryption for external connections and where latency issues would not result in an impact to the network.

practice.outcome: Protect sensitive information from unauthorized access.
practice.scope: All passwords, credentials, secrets, and other sensitive or controlled information
practice.risk_addressed:
Attackers can steal operational data from production environments for 
personal gain or to plan future operations. This information can include design documents, schedules, and other artifacts that provide insights into operations.
practice.recommend_action: Sensitive data, including credentials, are not stored in plaintext anywhere in the organization and can only be accessed by authenticated and authorized users. Credentials are stored in a secure manner, such as with a credential/password manager or vault, or other privileged account management solution. Identify critical physical and electronic file types and data to protect while in transit and at rest. This may include personally identifiable information and sensitive, proprietary or trade secret information (e.g., PLC program code, robot programs, computer-aided drafting  (CAD) or computer aided manufacturing (MAC) files, operating manuals and documentation, electrical diagrams, network diagrams, historical production data).

practice.outcome: Reduce the risk from embedded macros and similar executive code, a common and highly effective threat actor TTP.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries rely on users to open malicious files to execute code. Social engineering tactics could be used to convince users to open such files.
practice.recommend_action: A system-enforced policy that disables macros, or similar embedded code, by default on all devices to prevent automatic execution of code or application. If macros must be enabled in specific circumstances, there is a policy for authorized users to request that macros are enabled on specific assets.

practice.outcome: Policies and procedures exist to manage system configurations and changes that are consistent with industry-accepted hardening standards.
practice.risk_addressed:
Configuration and change management enables the organization 
to control frequent changes to its high-value assets so that disruptions are mitigated and benefits are optimized.
practice.recommend_action: Implement policies and processes to develop, document, and maintain secure configurations for technology platforms, aligning with industry-accepted system hardening standards. Additionally, they enforce configuration restrictions to prevent unauthorized changes. Technical configuration change control processes, prohibiting unauthorized changes unless approved are in-place. Test and document proposed changes in a non-production environment and analyze potential security impacts before implementation.

practice.outcome: Organizations reduce data loss and service disruption risks while efficiently managing, responding to, and recovering from cyberattacks to ensure continuous service delivery.
practice.scope: Organizational assets necessary for business operations
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers can disrupt critical systems to halt the delivery of products or services. They can also delete or remove built-in data and disable recovery services, preventing system recovery. Adversaries may turn off services designed to aid in recovering a corrupted system.
practice.recommend_action:
Develop a list of all maintained backups, including installation media, license keys, configuration information, and backup retention period of the information.Backup critical operations systems  in near-real-time, and frequently back up all systems necessary for operations at agreed-upon schedules.Securely store backups offsite and offline. Test backups and recovery on a recurring basis, no less than once per year.Before initiating restoration validate the integrity of backups and other 
assets intended for restoration. This verification process is to ensure that data is intact, accurate, and reliable, minimizing the risk of data corruption during the restoration process.Check restoration assets for indicators of compromise, file corruption, and other integrity issues before use.  Regularly test backup information to verify media reliability and information integrity.Stored information for OT assets includes at a minimum: configurations, roles, programmable logic controller (PLC), engineering drawings, and tools.

practice.outcome: More efficiently and effectively respond to cyberattacks and maintain service continuity.
practice.risk_addressed: Incomplete or inaccurate understanding of network topology inhibits effective incident response and recovery.
practice.recommend_action: Organizations maintain accurate documentation describing updated network topology and relevant information across all IT and OT networks. Network reviews should be performed and tracked on a annual basis and documentation updated when network topology changes are made.

practice.outcome:
Increase visibility into deployed technology assets, and reduce the likelihood of breach by users installing unapproved hardware, firmware, or 
software.
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers can manipulate products or delivery mechanisms before they reach the final consumer, aiming to compromise data or systems. They can target devices that move across ICS and external networks, typically brought in by authorized personnel but not permanently staying in the environment.
practice.recommend_action: Implement an administrative policy and  process that requires review, testing, and approval before new hardware, firmware, or software (software version) is installed or deployed. Organizations maintain a list of approved hardware, firmware, and software that includes specification of approved versions, when technically feasible.Consider additional requirements for organizations with OT environments when deploying patches and updates. This includes testing and validation to ensure they do not impact operational capabilities or safety.

practice.outcome: Enhance visibility to detect and respond to cyberattacks while ensuring security logs are protected from unauthorized access and tampering.
practice.risk_addressed: Adversaries can alter components within a victim's environment to disable defensive mechanisms. This includes impairing both preventative defenses like firewalls and anti-virus, as well as detection tools used to identify malicious behavior. This can affect both native and additional defenses set up by users and administrators.
practice.recommend_action: Administrative and security-focused logs (e.g., operating systems, applications, and services; intrusion detection systems/intrusion prevention systems, firewall, data loss prevention, virtual private network) are collected and stored for use in both detection and incident response activities (e.g., forensics). Typical events to be collected include maintenance functions (e.g., access control, configuration changes, backup and restore) OS functions and application (i.e., process) events. Logs are stored in a central system, such as a security information and event management tool or central database, and can only be accessed or modified by authorized and authenticated users. Logs are stored for a duration informed by risk or pertinent regulatory guidelines.  Security teams are notified when a critical log source is disabled.For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, network traffic and communications between those assets and other assets is collected.

practice.outcome: Prevent malicious actors from achieving initial access or data exfiltration via unauthorized portable media devices.
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers might infiltrate systems, including disconnected or air-gapped networks, by copying malware to removable media. They exploit Autorun features, causing the malware to execute once the media is inserted into a system.
practice.recommend_action:
Organizations maintain policies and processes to ensure that unauthorized media and hardware are not connected to IT and OT assets, such as limiting use of USB devices and removable media or disabling AutoRun. OT: When feasible, establish procedures to remove, disable, or otherwise secure physical ports to prevent the connection of unauthorized devices or establish procedures for granting 
access through approved exceptions.

practice.security_practice: No Exploitable Services on The Internet
practice.outcome: Unauthorized users cannot gain an initial system foothold by exploiting known weaknesses in internet-facing assets.
practice.scope: Organizational assets on the public internet
practice.risk_addressed: Attackers might exploit weaknesses in internet-facing hosts or systems to gain initial network access, targeting software bugs, temporary glitches, or misconfigurations.
practice.recommend_action: Minimize internet-facing assets whenever possible. Where necessary, prioritize keeping your software up to date with timely patches and updates. If unable to apply updates, ensure appropriate compensating controls are implemented to prevent common forms of exploitation.  All unnecessary OS applications, software (bloatware) and network protocols are disabled on internet-facing assets.Logically segment organization networks and cloud-based platforms according to trust boundaries and platform types (e.g., IT, IoT, OT, mobile, guests), and permit required communications only between segments.

practice.outcome: Monitoring for malware encompasses computing hardware, software, runtime environments, and their associated data to identify potentially adverse events.
practice.risk_addressed: Malicious software can involve payloads, droppers, backdoors, and more. Attackers use malware to maintain control of remote machines, evade defenses, and execute post-compromise actions.
practice.recommend_action: Implement signature-based mechanisms (relying on known patterns or signatures of malicious code, used by antivirus software to identify and block threats) and non-signature-based mechanisms (focusing on zero-day attacks, behavior, heuristics, or anomalies) to detect and eradicate malicious code at system endpoints. Ensure antivirus software is updated, active, and configured to automatically scan emails and removable media (e.g., flash drives) for ransomware and other malware.Using antivirus software with OT devices may require special practices, including compatibility checks, change management, and performance impact metrics. These practices should be employed to test new signatures and new versions of antivirus software.

practice.outcome: Incidents are declared when adverse events meet the specified incident criteria.
practice.risk_addressed: Initial Access, Privilege Escalation, Lateral Movement
practice.recommend_action:
Ensure the organization has defined clear criteria and process for adverse events.If an adverse event is suspected, follow the protocol outlined in the incident response plan to escalate the situation.Automate event information analysis as much as possible to extend the investigative timeline for managing suspected adverse events. This will give analysts the time and capacity to mitigate these events effectively.Conduct role-specific training that informs analysts of the proper protocols and procedures to take in the event of a suspected cyber incident.Organizations should account for OT-specific events 
and anomalies in their processes and environments. It's important to recognize that certain tools and alerts for behaviors or events that could indicate an intrusion might actually be normal within the OT environment.

practice.outcome: Coordinate crisis communication methods between internal and external organization partners and its critical suppliers.
practice.risk_addressed:
The inability to appropriately respond to incidents in a timely manner.

A compromise of a system, application or service that affects confidentiality, integrity, availability and/or safety.
practice.recommend_action: Securely share information consistent with response plans and information sharing agreements. Priorities for sharing information include preventing the spread of infections to other systems and networks.Regularly update senior leadership on the status of major incidents.Notify human resources when malicious insider activity has occurred.Establish and follow media communications procedures for incident response that comply with the organization’s policies on media interaction and information disclosure.Coordinating with partner organizations to share tactical and technical information on mitigating attacks across multiple entities is essential for enhancing security and resilience. This collaborative effort helps protect critical infrastructure from both cyber and physical threats.

practice.outcome: CISA and other organizations are better able to provide assistance or understand the broader scope of a cyberattack.
practice.risk_addressed: Without timely incident reporting, CISA and other groups are less able to assist affected organizations and lack critical insight into the broader threat landscape (such as whether a broader attack is occurring against a specific sector).
practice.recommend_action:
Organizations maintain codified policy and procedures on to whom and how to report all confirmed cybersecurity incidents to appropriate external entities (e.g., state/federal regulators or 
SRMA’s as required, ISAC/ISAO, as well as CISA).Known incidents are reported to CISA as well as other necessary parties within time frames directed by applicable regulatory guidance or in the absence of guidance, as soon as safely capable.
